title: Spin a rattleback the wrong way and it rocks to a stop, then spins backwards

cover.alt: A shiny bent spoon spinning on its curved back on a dark surface, its handle blurred by the motion.

body: A **rattleback** is a curved top that is subtly lopsided: its mass, or the axis it rolls about, is skewed relative to its shape. Spun in its preferred direction it simply spins. Spun the other way, it soon starts to rock end to end, the spin dies away, and it turns the other way, as if by itself. The skew couples the spinning and the rocking, so energy in one motion feeds the other. Some, like this bent spoon, reverse several times in a row.

slides.alt: A bent metal spoon spins on its rounded back on a dark surface. Twice it slows, rocks back and forth on the spot, and then starts spinning again in the opposite direction.
slides.caption: A bent spoon makes a homemade rattleback: as it spins on its back it slows, rocks, and sets off the other way, more than once.
slides.music: “Marty Gots a Plan” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

steps.label: It is spun against its preferred way
Its skewed shape turns spin into rocking
The rocking grows as the spin dies
Rocking turns back into spin, reversed

slides.heading: First described in the 1890s
slides.text: The first modern descriptions came in the 1890s, when Gilbert Walker wrote 'On a curious dynamical property of celts'. Celt is an old word for a stone tool shaped like an axe or adze, and rattlebacks are still sometimes called celts.

slides.heading: Which is not a name for a rattleback?
slides.explanation: Celt, wobble stone and druid stone are all names for the rattleback. A tippe top is a different toy, one that flips over onto its stem as it spins.

slides.question: Why do most rattlebacks only reverse when spun one way?
options: Friction stops them first the other way
slides.explanation: Spun the other way, friction and damping usually bring the top to a stop before the rocking has time to build up. A few rattlebacks do reverse in both directions.
